the questions of roots and routes, the relationship between the two and the impact of this relationship on the identity of modern American and contemporary Palestinian exiles.
the question: how do Palestinian and American expatriate authors represent their relationship with their homeland and their subsequent routes in their works?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the routes followed by the protagonists of both American and Palestinian writers are not the same.

while American expatriate authors represent the return to the US and their routes to be possible, Palestinian exiled authors represent the impossibility of return to Palestine and their routes to exile as inevitable.
Palestinian authors’ involuntary exile, the impossibility of their repatriation and the subsequent involuntary return to exile are all the result of the Israeli occupation and its policies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

while American expatriate authors have the choice to return to their roots and follow the route of repatriation, Palestinian exile authors have no choice and are forced to return to exile and follow the route back to exile.
while the modern American expatriates represent their return as possible, Palestinian authors describe homecoming as impossible.
the return of exiled Palestinians to Palestine is not only possible but also impossible.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Palestinian exilic writers, in their works, are more concerned with the impossibility of return and the impossibility of the returnees to reconnect to their roots than they are about the possibility of return and reconnection with the roots.
Palestinian exile is a unique experience in which the impossibility of returning home has become the norm.

while modern American writers have the choice to decide whether they want to go home or not, Palestinian exiled authors are unable to do so, as their return is not a matter of choice, but a matter of impossibility.
